title: 2 Corinthians
subtitle: Strength in weakness, and the ministry of reconciliation
lead: Second Corinthians is the most personal of Paul's letters. He writes to a church he founded, had hurt and been hurt by, and was now trying to win back. In it he explains why his travel plans changed, tells of the day he gave up hope of living, asks the Corinthians to forgive an offender, and describes his work as the ministry of a new covenant, a treasure carried in clay pots. He asks for money for the poor in Jerusalem (chapters 8 and 9), and in the last four chapters he turns on rivals he mocks as "super-apostles," boasts like a fool, tells of being caught up to the third heaven, and speaks of a thorn in his flesh.

No other letter shows Paul so exposed. Many of the best-known lines in the New Testament come from it: "treasure in clay pots" (4:7), "we walk by faith, not by what we see" (5:7), "new creation" (5:17), "be reconciled to God" (5:20), the cheerful giver (9:7), and power made perfect in weakness (12:9). Yet it is also a hard letter. Its argument jumps from topic to topic, it takes up Old Testament stories with a freedom that surprised its first readers, and scholars still argue about whether it is one letter or several pieced together. This Plain English study sets out the text, the debates and the traditions for readers of every church.
facts: Paul, undisputed. Timothy is named as co-sender (1:1). The letter was probably dictated; it does not name a scribe.
About AD 55 or 56 (some say 56 or 57), in the autumn, a year or so after 1 Corinthians. Dates vary by a year or two with the chronology of Paul's life.
Macedonia (2:13; 7:5; 9:2), perhaps Philippi, as later manuscript endings say; Paul was on his way to Corinth for his third visit (12:14; 13:1).
The church of God in Corinth and "all the saints throughout Achaia" (1:1): a church of mostly Gentile believers, some wealthy and many poor, in a Roman colony proud of its honor and wealth.
A letter, with sections of defense, thanksgiving, appeal and warning; parts are in the style of a legal defense, and the last four chapters use irony and a mock boast.
13 chapters, 257 verses (the closing blessing is 13:14 here and 13:13 in some Greek editions)
authorship: Second Corinthians is one of the letters nearly all scholars accept as Paul's own, with Romans, 1 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. Its personal detail (the escape from Damascus, 11:32–33; the thorn, 12:7; the collection) and its vocabulary match the other letters. No serious critic since the nineteenth century has denied it.

Whether Paul wrote 2 Corinthians as one letter is much debated. The break at 2:13/7:5, the sudden warning of 6:14–7:1, the two appeals for the collection (8 and 9) and the change of tone at chapter 10 have led many scholars to think that the book as we have it is made of two or more letters. The common theories: (1) chapters 10–13 are a separate letter written after chapters 1–9 (Thrall's commentary takes 1–9 as one letter and 10–13 as a later, separate one); (2) chapters 10–13 are the earlier "tearful letter" (Hausrath, Kennedy, Bornkamm); (3) 2:14–7:4 is a separate letter; (4) 6:14–7:1 is a fragment from another letter, or is not by Paul; (5) chapters 8 and 9 are two letters about the collection; (6) the letter is one whole, written over a period of time, with the change at chapter 10 explained by new reports reaching Paul in the interval (Harris, Garland and Barnett defend the unity of the whole). Both sides can be read in the notes.
Timothy is named as sender and helped found the church (1:19; Acts 18:5). The letter is mostly in the first person, and scholars debate whether "we" means Paul alone.

audience.to: The church of God in Corinth and the saints throughout Achaia (1:1): a church that Paul founded about AD 50–52 (Acts 18:1–18) in the Roman colony of Corinth. Most of its members were Gentiles, from every level of society: a few wealthy members, such as Erastus the city treasurer (Romans 16:23), and many poor, with slaves and freed people. The city prized honor, patronage and eloquent speech. Paul had written to the church at least twice already (1 Corinthians 5:9; 1 Corinthians), had made a short and painful visit, and had sent a harsh letter, most likely through Titus (2:1–4; 7:8–12). Titus had brought good news of repentance (7:6–16), but the church was divided: most had come back to Paul, but a group, perhaps encouraged by outside preachers who carried letters and claimed Jewish credentials (3:1; 11:4, 22), still questioned his authority.
audience.why: To rebuild the relationship, to defend his ministry against the charge that his weakness and changed plans showed he was not a true apostle, to finish the collection for Jerusalem, and to warn the church against rivals before his third visit. Knowing the audience changes the reading: much of the letter is an answer to specific accusations (that he was unreliable, a poor speaker, a man who did not take pay, a man whose body showed signs of weakness). When Paul speaks of weakness as the place where power appears (4:7; 12:9), he is answering critics who thought a true apostle would look strong.
views: Many scholars take the rivals of 11:4, 22 as Jewish-Christian missionaries who came to Corinth with letters, boasting of their Hebrew background and their visions (Barrett, Thrall).
Georgi argued that the rivals presented themselves as wonder-working "divine men" in the Hellenistic Jewish style, so that Paul's weakness looked like proof that he was not one.
A few scholars think that the pressure came mostly from within the church (a Corinthian taste for status and rhetoric), with the visitors only a catalyst.

outline: Blessing for the God of all comfort; the trouble in Asia
A defense of his plans; the painful visit and the tearful letter; forgiving the offender; Troas and Macedonia

The ministry of the new covenant and the call to open hearts: the victory parade, the letter on hearts, the veil of Moses, treasure in clay pots, the earthly tent, new creation and reconciliation, the appeal of 6:1–13, the warning of 6:14–7:1
The collection for Jerusalem: the example of Macedonia, "though he was rich" (8:9), the cheerful giver (9:7)
Paul and the super-apostles: the weapons of the war, the fool's boast, the lists of sufferings, the escape from Damascus, the third heaven, the thorn, the warning of a third visit

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads the letter against Paul's life after Ephesus (the trouble in Asia, Macedonia, Titus), Roman Corinth with its honor, patronage and rhetoric, the crisis after 1 Corinthians (the painful visit and the tearful letter), the collection for Jerusalem and the political and social world behind the boasting, the escape from Damascus under Aretas, and the lists of hardships. Used by historians and archaeologists such as Murphy-O'Connor and Danker.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the letter was made and who the people in it were: whether it is one letter or several joined together, whether 6:14–7:1 is an interpolation, who the opponents (the "super-apostles") were, what the tearful letter was, and what the manuscripts read. Associated with Bornkamm, Georgi, Betz, Thrall and Harris.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as speech: its irony, its antitheses and paradoxes (strength in weakness), the long sentences of 1:3–7, the hardship lists, the fool's speech of chapters 11–12, and the way Paul uses Scripture (Exodus 34, Jeremiah 31, Isaiah 49, Psalm 116).

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads Paul as a Jew writing to Gentiles: the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 and the veil of Moses, the Jewish idea of a heavenly journey (the third heaven), Paul's thirty-nine lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3), the Hebrew credentials of the rivals, and the post-Holocaust questions about supersession. Associated with Gager, Nanos, Fredriksen, Boyarin and the Jewish Annotated New Testament.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as the churches have: Chrysostom's homilies, Augustine on the letter and the Spirit, Aquinas, Luther and Calvin on the atonement and the covenant, Wesley, Orthodox readings of glory and theosis, and Catholic teaching on penance and judgment.

sections.b:
Read it as the sound of one side of a conversation. Paul answers charges that we hear only from his replies: that he changed his plans lightly (1:17), that he needs letters of introduction (3:1), that he is a poor speaker (10:10; 11:6), that he refuses pay because he is not a true apostle (11:7–11; 12:13), that he is a coward at a distance and bold only in letters (10:1, 10). Behind them stands a church that had divided over him.

The letter moves in waves: thanks and relief (1–7), an appeal for money (8–9), and a stern defense and warning (10–13). Each wave keeps one thought: God's power appears in weakness. That is why the "treasure in clay pots" (4:7) and the "thorn in the flesh" (12:7–10) belong together.

sections.h: The timeline of Paul and Corinth
sections.b: Paul founded the church in about AD 50–52 (Acts 18). He then wrote an earlier letter (1 Corinthians 5:9), 1 Corinthians (about AD 54–55), made a short painful visit, wrote a tearful letter through Titus, met Titus in Macedonia, and wrote 2 Corinthians (about AD 55–56). A third visit followed, in the winter when Romans was written (Acts 20:2–3). The study page for chapter 1 sets out the steps, and which of them are certain.

sections.h: The key words in this Plain
sections.b: The Plain gives the same English for the same Greek in key places. Paraklesis, comfort (1:3–7), is one root with many meanings (comfort, encourage, urge, beg). Katargeo, "set aside" (3:7, 11, 13, 14), is one verb that can mean fade, end or lose power; the "passed away" of 5:17 is a different verb. Arrabon is "down payment" (1:22; 5:5), as in Ephesians 1:14. Katallasso, "reconcile" (5:18–20). Diakonia, "ministry" (3:7–9; 4:1; 5:18; 6:3), and doulos, "slave" (4:5), are kept apart. Thlipsis is "trouble," as in Romans. "Brothers" is kept for adelphoi, as in Acts and Romans, with a gloss. Sarx is "flesh," never "sinful nature."

sections.h: How Jews and Christians have read the letter
sections.b: The chapters on the veil of Moses (3:7–18) and on the old covenant (3:14) are the passages most used in Christian arguments with Judaism, and most read in Jewish discussion of Paul. Jewish readers point out that Exodus 34 does not say the glory faded, that Jeremiah's new covenant is made with Israel and Judah, and that Paul's account of the veil goes beyond the story. Christian readers have long taken the passage as proof that the covenant of Moses is ended, and it has been used against Jews. Many scholars now read it as about two ministries, and not the fate of a people, and read Paul as still honoring the Law and hoping for Israel (Romans 7:12; 11:26). Paul's own claim to be an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham and a Hebrew (11:22) is part of the same letter. Both readings and the cards on 3:6 and 3:14 are in this study.

This Plain follows the SBL Greek New Testament, checked against NA28, the Tyndale House Greek New Testament, the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus behind the KJV. The notes give each place where the text affects the English, for example 1:6 (the order of the clauses), 1:12 ("holiness" or "simplicity"), 4:6, 5:3 ("put on" or "take off") and 5:17 ("all things"). The oldest Greek manuscript of the letter is commonly said to be Papyrus 46 (about AD 200), which contains most of 2 Corinthians, and the great codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s) also contain it (as commonly reported; not rechecked here). The variants give editions only, and manuscript lists are in the NA28/UBS5 apparatus and Metzger. 2 Corinthians 13:14 is 13:13 in some Greek editions; the text is the same.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the letter's own story shadows Exodus 32–34
spec.body:
The story of Moses after Sinai runs: the people break the covenant (the golden calf, Exodus 32), Moses breaks the tablets and pleads for them, God threatens to withdraw (33:3), Moses asks to see God's glory (33:18), the tablets are renewed (34:1–28), and Moses comes down with a shining face and a veil (34:29–35). Paul's own story in 2 Corinthians has a loosely similar shape: a break (the painful visit), a plea (the tearful letter), a threat to withdraw (the cancelled visits), a restoration (Titus's news, 7:6–16), and then an argument about glory and a veil (chapter 3). If so, when Paul writes about Moses in chapter 3, he is not choosing a random Old Testament story but reading his own recent history through Exodus 32–34. The reading also explains why the Moses passage comes where it does, right after the question "who is up to this task?" (2:16), which is how a mediator might feel after a broken covenant.

This is my own suggestion. It rests on the order of events in the letter and on the verbal links in chapter 3 to Exodus 32–34 that Hafemann has argued. The analogy is loose: the Corinthians are not shown as breaking a covenant like the golden calf, since the letter says only that they grieved and then repented (7:6–16). I have not seen the whole story of the letter set beside the whole of Exodus 32–34 in the commentaries I know.

prompts: A plain clay jar, cracked at one side, sitting on a worn wooden table in a harbor-city workshop at Corinth; a warm gold light spills out through the cracks and falls across scrolls and a pair of tent-maker's tools; behind it, through an open arch, the Acrocorinth hill and the sea. Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment, with ancient manuscript borders, cave-painting ochre and soft modern watercolor; soft edges, no hard rectangle.

Moses on a rock at the foot of Sinai with his face shining like a sun drawn in ochre rays, a woven veil held in his hand, the Israelites in the valley shielding their eyes; at the edge of the picture a modern figure with an uncovered face looks at a polished bronze mirror that glows. Style: hand-sketched on aged parchment, manuscript border of vines, cave-painting figures and soft modern watercolor; soft edges.

A Roman triumphal procession winding through a city: a general in a chariot with laurel, captives with their hands tied, incense rising from braziers, and among the captives a small tired figure in a plain cloak carrying a scroll, with a quiet smile; behind them a crowd and a temple. Style: sketched onto old rolled parchment, ochre and charcoal, ancient manuscript borders mixed with modern ink and wash; soft edges.
reading: Margaret E. Thrall, A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians (ICC, 2 vols., 1994, 2000)
The fullest English commentary: careful on the Greek, fair to the partition theories, and generous with the history of interpretation.
Murray J. Harris, The Second Epistle to the Corinthians (NIGTC, 2005)
A detailed Greek commentary that defends the unity of the letter and weighs the textual and grammatical questions closely.
A readable evangelical commentary that argues for the letter's unity and gives much background on Corinth.
Paul Barnett, The Second Epistle to the Corinthians (NICNT, 1997)
A clear historical commentary that places the letter within Paul's life and the Corinthian crisis.
Victor Paul Furnish, II Corinthians (Anchor Bible 32A, 1984)
A well-balanced critical commentary, helpful on the structure and the theology of reconciliation.
Scott J. Hafemann, Paul, Moses, and the History of Israel (1995)
A detailed study of 2 Corinthians 3, reading it against Exodus 32–34.
Dieter Georgi, The Opponents of Paul in Second Corinthians (1986)
The classic argument that Paul's rivals were Hellenistic Jewish wonder-workers.
John T. Fitzgerald, Cracks in an Earthen Vessel (1988)
On Paul's lists of hardships in the Corinthian letters and their Greek and Stoic background.
